evidence.quote: A skill document and a LoRA can carry the same behaviour, but they are not equally useful. evidence.quote: LLM judges increasingly serve as quality gates for code changes that have no test oracle, but a judge prompt must be calibrated for its task and recalibrated as the system it judges evolves, while hand labels for the calibration are resource intensive and go stale. Development workflows emit outcome labels for free (tests pass or fail, changes land or are abandoned), but these labels are noisy. We present AutoRefine, a loop that rewrites a deployable judge’s prompt to reproduce outcome labels, with an informed teacher that sees the judge’s input plus the outcome, explains each label it keeps, and abstains when the outcome cannot be explained from what the judge sees. On a held-out dataset with an execution oracle, calibration raised chance-corrected agreement (Scott’s π \pi ) from 0.36 to 0.60. On a deployed agent’s outcome labels, with 25% flipped at random to introduce noise, the teacher set aside flipped fail labels at more than twice the rate of genuine ones, cutting overall label noise from 25% to 20%. Recalibrating that agent’s judge using AutoRefine raised its agreement with merge/abandon outcomes on 17 independently held-out diffs from the current workflow ( π \pi 0.16 to 0.51); on 16 diffs from older workflows, the previous judge stayed ahead, illustrating the need for recalibration as the agent evolves. By abstaining, the teacher not only removes noisy labels but also flags changes whose outcome the judge’s input cannot explain, telling a team when a judge needs better inputs rather than a better prompt.

evidence.quote: The loop (Fig. 1 ) is an iterative optimizer over the judge’s prompt. The prompt plays the role of the parameters, agreement with the labels on the training split is the objective, disagreement analysis supplies the update direction, and a validation split decides when to stop. Each iteration runs the current prompt on the training split and scores its verdicts with Scott’s π \pi [ 4 ] , which corrects raw agreement for the agreement expected by chance from the pooled verdict and label distribution, so a judge that always predicts the majority class scores at or below zero ( − 0.08 -0.08 on our oracle test split). For every disagreement, an LLM (Claude Opus 4.7 in our runs) reads the judge’s verdict and reasoning next to the label and any teacher justification and proposes edits. The edits must be balanced, so every new reason to fail is paired with a reason to pass, which keeps the judge from drifting toward rejecting everything. A second call applies the edits under a length cap. For rubric judges, which emit a weighted score, the decision threshold is chosen on the training split. A separate validation split, never curated, selects the final prompt; the loop stops at a target agreement, when no disagreements remain, or at a maximum number of iterations (five in our runs, on training splits of 125 to 127 diffs). The agent’s patches are recorded once and replayed, so calibration never reruns the agent under test.

evidence.quote: We design a controlled simulation study of agentic robot self-learning across five contact-rich VABAR manipulation tasks Xie et al. (2026b) and four longer-horizon MimicGen tasks Mandlekar et al. (2023) . Holding the overall self-learning harness fixed, we systematically vary four components of the learning loop: model capability, skill prior, feedback structure, and curriculum, as illustrated in Figure 2 . Across these studies, we find that self-learning is limited less by the availability of useful information than by the agent’s ability to turn the information into effective policy updates. More execution feedback is not necessarily more useful: feedback is most effective when aligned with semantically meaningful policy decisions rather than reported at the finest temporal resolution. Similarly, world-frame states contain all the information needed for manipulation, yet agents often fail to recover task-relevant object-relative and functional relationships unless these are made explicit. Even when agents identify local geometric errors, they often struggle to translate them into coherent collision-aware motion plans. We find that this limitation can also affect curriculum design: agents tend to preserve and patch policy structure inherited from earlier stages rather than fundamentally reorganize it, so privileged learning can either provide a useful initialization or constrain later learning when the inherited policy depends on privileged precision or brittle manipulation strategies. Our results further suggest that progress in agentic robot self-learning comes from the better structures of skills, feedback, and state representations and the learned physical reasoning ability from the underlying models.

evidence.quote: Natural language offers an intuitive way to direct a virtual crowd while a simulation is running. Backtests inside a model's training window therefore cannot be certified leak-free by self-report, instruction or stated cutoff. These findings motivate behavioral measurement of temporal knowledge boundaries, and FinDendro provides a benchmark and procedure for selecting backtest periods based on demonstrated factual knowledge.

evidence.quote: Abstract: Learning the continuous-time evolution of nonlinear dynamical systems relies on trajectory-based objectives, which require simulating the learned dynamics during training and backpropagating through the numerical scheme, at a cost that grows with the rollout horizon. We show that trajectory-based objectives degenerate as the rollout horizon increases, hindering gradient-based optimization, and that the numerical scheme biases the learned dynamics by constraining the spectrum of the learned Jacobian to its absolute stability region. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Velocity Matching (VM), a simulation-free objective that relies on piecewise-linear interpolation and stochastic collocation, and approximates the velocity population risk to second order in the sampling step. We develop a theoretical framework for velocity-based learning, introducing stability estimates that control trajectory errors in terms of velocity errors, which enable us to establish universal and continuous-time approximation results when the learned velocity field is parameterized by deep neural networks. Building on a bias-variance decomposition of the VM objective, we show that its higher-order approximation of the velocity population risk yields a consistent minimizer; that it relates to the residual of an A-stable continuous-stage Runge-Kutta scheme, thus connecting VM to implicit integration without requiring any implicit solve; and that it implicitly matches the action of the learned Jacobian to that of the true one along the observed trajectories, without requiring access to the underlying velocity field or its Jacobian. Numerical experiments on nonlinear ordinary differential equations and semi-discretized time-dependent partial differential equations show that VM improves accuracy over trajectory-based objectives, while avoiding both the cost of simulation and the instabilities of long rollouts.

evidence.quote: Abstract: Protein motif scaffolding benchmarks assess whether generative models can build scaffolds around functionally important residues. Their conclusions depend on which motifs are tested and which criteria define success. Existing benchmarks typically use small hand-curated motif sets and static refolding criteria, but protein function often depends on conformational ensembles and transitions. Here, we address both benchmark scope and success criteria. We introduce BILBY-PRO, a systematically derived benchmark of structurally conserved functional motifs from PROSITE-linked experimental structures, comprising 220 cases from 174 PROSITE motif-pattern entries. Evaluating six recent scaffold-generation models reveals distinct patterns in target coverage and unique-solution yield: RFDiffusion and Proteina solve more targets, whereas ESM3 produces more unique successful scaffolds on the targets it solves. We further introduce BILBY-MD, a reference-based all-atom molecular dynamics evaluation framework. Applied to statically solved designs from the original MotifBench benchmark, it compares motif drift, scaffold drift, motif-contact preservation, and motif-dihedral free-energy landscapes against reference simulations. Of 55 statically solved model-problem pairs, 31 satisfy our MD-supported criterion and only 8 pass all checks. Compact, self-contained motifs are often MD-supported, whereas interface-like or context-dependent motifs fail more frequently. Static refolding success therefore provides useful evidence of local motif recovery but does not establish dynamical fidelity of the full scaffold. BILBY highlights three complementary axes of motif-scaffolding evaluation: target coverage, unique-solution yield, and MD-supported dynamical fidelity.
